entries.short_title: Calibrates reality through standards and responsibility

sections.title: The overall pattern
sections.lead: If this candidate fits, attention may repeatedly return to standards, responsibility, and what could be improved.
paragraphs: When rules are vague or quality slips, you may first look for what would make the situation correct before addressing disappointment. That sequence across work, home, and private tasks is more informative than one instance of conscientiousness.

The protected need may be to act with integrity and remain accountable, rather than to be flawless. If standards relax easily in low-risk settings or tighten only under evaluation, role demands may explain the behavior better.
points: Repeatedly noticing deviation, ownership, and correctable gaps supports this candidate more than one isolated behavior.
If role accountability or a realistic need to prevent rework explains the pattern better, a stable type hypothesis deserves less weight.
sections.reflection_question: Recall one episode when standards slip, ownership is vague, or a deliverable still contains flaws. Where did your attention go first? What supports this candidate, and what points instead to the counterexample that you can stop naturally when the stakes are low?

sections.title: What draws attention and what you protect
sections.lead: You may notice standards, responsibility, and what could be improved earlier than people around you and allocate effort from there.
paragraphs: While others are still debating direction, you may already separate non-negotiable standards from details likely to create rework. The protected concern is often reliability and responsibility, not neatness alone.
In a low-risk task with no stated rules, voluntarily defining completion criteria supports this candidate. Doing so only under formal evaluation points more strongly to role demand.
points: The first object of attention can reveal an effort to act with integrity and dependable standards.
Test that possibility against actual trade-offs while ruling out role accountability or a realistic need to prevent rework.
sections.reflection_question: In a situation when standards slip, ownership is vague, or a deliverable still contains flaws, what were you trying hardest to preserve? Which observable consequences help separate material risk from personal preference?

sections.title: Outer expression and the need beneath it
sections.lead: The visible move may be to correct the deviation or clarify the rule before naming disappointment; the less spoken need may be to act with integrity without making flawlessness the price of self-respect.
paragraphs: Under pressure, you may check more often, correct details, tighten expectations, or become less flexible in order to restore order. That response can protect quality, but in a low-risk situation it can also narrow your options. This is an observable tendency, not a diagnosis or a confirmed defense mechanism.

Your effort to prevent errors may be heard as criticism or fault-finding. That possibility is a communication hypothesis: check what you intended, what the other person heard, and whether the risk was clear.
points: The visible move may be to check the rule and correct the problem; its purpose still requires contextual and first-person evidence.
Even when the aim is to act with integrity and dependable standards, another person’s reported impact remains independent evidence.
sections.reflection_question: Choose an interaction when standards slip, ownership is vague, or a deliverable still contains flaws in which someone saw your behavior but may not have understood its purpose. What did you hope to protect, and what alternative explanation did their response add?

sections.title: How emotion reinforces the habitual loop
sections.lead: A possible habitual sequence is to spot a defect, contain irritation, tighten expectations, then scan for the next defect.
paragraphs: Possible pressure cues include missed responsibilities, confusing expectations, relaxed standards, overlooked problems, or effort that does not produce a dependable result. These are situations to observe; the report cannot determine what you fear or turn an inferred concern into psychological fact.
Early signals may include repeated checking, sharper reactions to small deviations, difficulty recognizing completion, or physical tension.
points: A loop around deviation, ownership, and correctable gaps narrows through interpretation, emotion, and action rather than appearing all at once.
The pause before you check the rule and correct the problem is the point where another response may still be available.
sections.reflection_question: The last time when standards slip, ownership is vague, or a deliverable still contains flaws, in what order did emotion, interpretation, and action occur? If you paused at the second step, what different response would still have been available?

sections.title: How to recognize the pattern without mistyping
sections.lead: A mistyping risk is that professional rigor, role accountability, or a temporary high-stakes period can resemble this pattern.
paragraphs: You may label every correction as responsibility without separating material risk from preference or aesthetics. Ask what the correction actually protects, what evidence supports the risk, and what would happen if the detail remained imperfect.

If Type 1 doesn’t emerge as a major clue this time, think of it as a less prominent pattern: Watch to see if you’re less proactive in using standards, closures, and long-term responsibilities to calibrate your actions when rules are vague, quality drops, or responsibility boundaries are unclear. It's not a judgment that you lack a sense of principle.
points: Attention to deviation, ownership, and correctable gaps across work, relationships, and private choices carries more weight than behavior in one role.
Keep role accountability or a realistic need to prevent rework as a serious competing explanation.
sections.reflection_question: Around the distinction between material risk from personal preference, which evidence repeats across settings, and which similar behavior is better explained by role, culture, temporary strain, or a learned habit?

sections.title: How to read adjacent-type influences
sections.lead: Type 1, The Reformer is adjacent to Type 9, The Peacemaker and Type 2, The Helper. Adjacency theory supports comparison, but a second-place score or one behavior cannot determine a wing.
paragraphs: Compare the recurring attention behind standards, responsibility, and what could be improved with what each adjacent type protects; do not convert ranking into identity.

sections.title: How the pattern helps when capacity is available
sections.lead: With enough capacity, this pattern may help you turn vague expectations into workable standards and catch preventable failures early.
paragraphs: With more capacity and choice, when you explain what a standard protects—quality, fairness, or safety—others can understand your persistence as stewardship rather than fault-finding.
When you explain what a standard protects—quality, fairness, or safety—others can understand your persistence as stewardship rather than fault-finding.
points: With enough capacity, attention to deviation, ownership, and correctable gaps can become a concrete contribution.
A resourceful expression can act with integrity and dependable standards while leaving room for other methods.
sections.reflection_question: In one situation when standards slip, ownership is vague, or a deliverable still contains flaws where you still had enough capacity, whom did this attention pattern help and what problem did it solve? Which condition made it a resource rather than an automatic response?

sections.title: When the same tendency becomes costly
sections.lead: When flexibility drops, the same tendency may promote preferences into principles and keep everyone under continuous review.
paragraphs: Under heavier load, even when the work is sufficient, you may feel pulled to add more effort. Separate high-consequence risks from details that can safely remain imperfect. This is an observation cue, not a level assignment or diagnosis.
Even when the work is sufficient, you may feel pulled to add more effort. Separate high-consequence risks from details that can safely remain imperfect.
points: Immediate usefulness does not remove later cost; a key turning point is when you turn low-stakes preferences into principles.
Use downstream effects to distinguish that cost from role accountability or a realistic need to prevent rework, not the type label.
sections.reflection_question: When did the same strategy recently pass its point of benefit? Record the immediate gain, the later cost, and whether the counterexample—you can stop naturally when the stakes are low—would have served the situation better.

sections.title: Where intention and impact may diverge
sections.lead: The intention may be constructive, yet an attempt to protect quality can land as criticism or distrust.
paragraphs: When you explain what a standard protects—quality, fairness, or safety—others can understand your persistence as stewardship rather than fault-finding. The same attention pattern can become costly when even when the work is sufficient, you may feel pulled to add more effort. Separate high-consequence risks from details that can safely remain imperfect.
If the first message is what needs fixing, others may miss the care behind it. State the shared aim before the correction.
points: Wanting to act with integrity and dependable standards does not ensure that efforts to check the rule and correct the problem will be understood that way.
Around deviation, ownership, and correctable gaps, separate intention, observable behavior, and impact to create a repair path.
sections.reflection_question: Choose an interaction when standards slip, ownership is vague, or a deliverable still contains flaws where intent and impact diverged. What did you mean to protect, what did the other person receive, and what clarification might have narrowed the gap?

sections.title: How care is expressed and what treatment matters
sections.lead: You may show care through reliability, careful follow-through, and fixing what could cause harm.
paragraphs: Reliability, remembering details, and repairing problems may be ways you express care. Check whether the other person experiences those actions as support, correction, or both; type theory cannot infer either person’s needs. In conflict, you may begin with facts, standards, and what needs to change. Add your feelings, the other person’s perspective, and the actual stakes so the discussion does not collapse into a verdict about who is right.
In a relationship with clear agreements and clear responsibilities, it may be easier for you to show that you care by being punctual, honoring your obligations, and handling problems cleanly.
points: Care may be expressed when you check the rule and correct the problem, but a type cannot specify what the other person needs.
Asking whether support landed also tests whether the aim to act with integrity and dependable standards was central in that moment.
sections.reflection_question: In a relationship where material risk from personal preference may matter, how did you recently express care? Ask whether it landed as support, pressure, or something else. How did the answer differ from your expectation?

sections.title: Recurring relationship difficulties
sections.lead: A recurring relationship difficulty may be to revisit who was responsible and what would have been fair or appropriate.
paragraphs: You may be protecting quality or fairness, but if it's an issue right from the start, the other person may feel negated at first. First ask the other person if they are willing to listen to feedback, and then explain the impact of your concerns; repair in the relationship also requires the other person to be willing to respond, rather than just relying on you to make the standards clearer.

Repeated questions about rules, timing, or commitments may be an attempt to make the relationship dependable, but the immediate situation may also carry real risk. Ask which consequence matters most before interpreting the questions as criticism.
points: A relational problem may recur when you turn low-stakes preferences into principles, not only with one particular person.
Boundaries, power, and communication history may explain the conflict better than attention to deviation, ownership, and correctable gaps.
sections.reflection_question: Which relationship difficulty recurs with different people? Which steps involve material risk from personal preference, and which are better explained by boundaries, power, or communication habits?

sections.title: How conflict escalates and how repair can begin
sections.lead: Conflict may escalate when you enter through facts and principles, then sound increasingly like a verdict when urgency rises.
paragraphs: In conflict, you may begin with facts, standards, and what needs to change. Add your feelings, the other person’s perspective, and the actual stakes so the discussion does not collapse into a verdict about who is right.
I just seemed to be finding fault. In fact, what I was worried about was how this incident would affect the next steps. Let me explain the impact clearly first.
points: As conflict escalates, concern with deviation, ownership, and correctable gaps may crowd out feelings and the shared aim.
Repair turns the wish to act with integrity and dependable standards into a bounded request rather than a personality judgment.
sections.reflection_question: Review one conflict intensified by the tension between material risk from personal preference. What was the first observable signal, and where could repair begin with facts, feelings, and a bounded request?

sections.title: How tasks move and the conditions that help
sections.lead: In task settings, you may tend to define the standard, material risk, and completion criteria before moving steadily.
paragraphs: At work, your attention may go first to standards, process gaps, ownership, and acceptable quality. This can explain why calibration matters to you, but it does not establish competence, job fit, or performance.

When requirements, acceptance criteria or delivery standards are still vague, it may be easier for you to break them into checklists, process nodes and review questions to help the team reduce rework.
points: The tendency to check the rule and correct the problem can support quality or pace at the right task stage.
As the stage changes, reassess whether investment in deviation, ownership, and correctable gaps still fits.
sections.reflection_question: During a task stage when standards slip, ownership is vague, or a deliverable still contains flaws, how did this way of working improve quality or pace? At what later stage did it need to be complemented by a different strategy?

sections.title: Information, feedback, and friction in collaboration
sections.lead: In collaboration, you may value dependable handoffs and closed loops, with low tolerance for ambiguous ownership.
paragraphs: When you are quick to point out omissions, discrepancies, or inconsistencies, collaborators may first hear "being corrected" rather than hearing that you are protecting the quality of your delivery. A more negotiable approach is to first explain the risks, acceptance criteria, or common goals associated with this piece of feedback, and then distinguish between the parts that must be corrected and those that can be observed later; this is just a clue to communication friction, and it does not mean that you are necessarily picky or that others are necessarily resistant to feedback.
By explaining the risks, impacts, and shared goals before asking a question, you reduce the chance that others will interpret your warning as critical.
points: Collaboration can strain when concern with deviation, ownership, and correctable gaps is not translated into usable information and feedback.
Repair goals, ownership, and communication design before ruling out role accountability or a realistic need to prevent rework.
sections.reflection_question: In a recent collaboration friction involving material risk from personal preference, was the missing ingredient information, feedback design, ownership, or psychological safety? What evidence shows that type need not explain it?

sections.title: Leading and being led: authority, boundaries, and interaction
sections.lead: Around authority, you may over-check when leading and seek explicit standards and rationale when being led.
paragraphs: When you are in a leading, coordinating or reminding position, your influence may come from clarifying goals, standards, responsibilities and review mechanisms, so that delivery does not rely solely on personal awareness. It is suitable for use in scenarios where quality risks are high and processes are prone to drift; however, this only affects style cues and does not mean that the system determines that you have leadership capabilities or are suitable for management positions.

When others need to collaborate with you, assign tasks, or make requests, it may be easier to keep you engaged by clearly stating boundaries, priorities, acceptance criteria, and where trial and error are allowed. What is described here is a preference for collaboration. It is not a general prescription for management methods, nor does it necessarily mean that you need a high-control environment.
points: Clear authority makes it less necessary to act with integrity and dependable standards through guessing or repeated escalation.
Explicit decision rights and stopping conditions help prevent the pattern from starting to turn low-stakes preferences into principles.
sections.reflection_question: In delegating, leading, or being managed when standards slip, ownership is vague, or a deliverable still contains flaws, which authority or stopping condition remained unclear? What observable outcome would change if it were explicit?

sections.title: How the habit intensifies or changes under pressure
sections.lead: As pressure rises, you may narrow acceptable options, magnify defects, and reduce tolerance for mistakes.
paragraphs: A minor issue begins to feel urgent before its actual impact has been checked.
After finishing, your attention stays on the remaining gaps rather than what already meets the requirement.
points: Pressure may amplify the impulse to check the rule and correct the problem until it begins to turn low-stakes preferences into principles.
Sleep, workload, and role accountability or a realistic need to prevent rework must be checked alongside a type hypothesis.
sections.reflection_question: As pressure rose when standards slip, ownership is vague, or a deliverable still contains flaws, which action intensified first? What did it protect, when did it narrow choice, and could sleep, workload, or real risk explain it better?

sections.title: What becomes possible when safety increases
sections.lead: With more safety, you may allow several sound approaches and make room for ease without treating it as negligence.
paragraphs: With enough authority and resources, you may translate problems into clearer processes, documentation, or review practices rather than stopping at criticism.
Your caution can be valuable when safety, commitments, or long-term trust are at stake. In lower-risk situations, distinguish necessary standards from extra effort.
points: When safety increases, the impulse to check the rule and correct the problem is no longer the only familiar response.
Look for flexibility while attending to deviation, ownership, and correctable gaps, not evidence that you have become another type.
sections.reflection_question: When you felt safe and unhurried, did a different response appear—for example, you can stop naturally when the stakes are low? How could you tell that safety, rather than a different task, accounted for the change?

sections.title: Growth means adding choice, not becoming another type
sections.lead: Growth can mean learning to separate non-negotiable principles from preferences and practice responsible sufficiency.
paragraphs: For one non-critical task this week, define the minimum acceptable standard, the risks that truly need protection, and the details that may remain unfinished. Review the factual outcome without turning every flaw into a judgment about yourself.
Log the other issues without fixing them immediately, then see which ones still matter the next day.
points: Growth adds an optional step before you check the rule and correct the problem; it does not require erasing the original tendency.
Use seven days of evidence to test whether the new choice can act with integrity and dependable standards without the familiar cost.
sections.reflection_question: The next time when standards slip, ownership is vague, or a deliverable still contains flaws, what small choice could you add without discarding your existing strength? What behavioral evidence after seven days would count as useful?

sections.title: Early signals and routes back to choice
sections.lead: Early signals may include a stream of “shoulds,” a tightened jaw, or silent rework.
paragraphs: Start by separating critical risks from non-critical imperfections. Choose one low-stakes detail to leave alone, then compare the actual outcome with what you predicted.
Sort issues by consequence, then address only the deviation that most affects the outcome.

growth_actions.title: Correct one material issue and defer the rest
growth_actions.instruction: Choose a reversible task with several visible flaws. Rank them by material risk, correct only the first, place the rest on tomorrow’s list, and stop at the criterion set in advance.
growth_actions.observable_outcome: Record whether deferred issues caused harm, how long delivery took, and whether physical tension eased after stopping. If material risk grew, revise the risk rule instead of forcing the exercise.

growth_actions.title: Ask what risk the other person sees before stating the standard
growth_actions.instruction: Before stating a standard, ask what risk the other person sees and summarize the answer in one sentence. Then separate required correction from personal preference.
growth_actions.observable_outcome: Note any information you had missed, whether the discussion reached a shared standard sooner, and whether you still expressed the boundary clearly.

growth_actions.title: Define “good enough” for one low-risk task
growth_actions.instruction: Before a low-risk task, define minimum acceptance, one risk that must be controlled, and two details that may remain unfinished. Deliver when those conditions are met without raising the bar afterward.
growth_actions.observable_outcome: Compare the written standard with the outcome, any rework, and whether others could use the result. Mark which feared imperfections never became consequential.

growth_actions.title: Observe one acceptable outcome after choosing not to correct immediately
growth_actions.instruction: Leave one safe, repairable imperfection untouched for twenty-four hours. Record each urge to correct it and the reason without suppressing the discomfort.
growth_actions.observable_outcome: After twenty-four hours, check the actual consequence, attention consumed, and other people’s responses. If the issue mattered, document the evidence rather than calling the exercise a failure.

growth_actions.title: Turn one criticism into a specific request
growth_actions.instruction: Take one recent criticism and rewrite it as an observable fact, its impact, and a bounded request. Leave room for a response without adding a moral judgment.
growth_actions.observable_outcome: Keep the original and revised versions, then note whether the request could be answered, whether conflict intensity changed, and whether it addressed a material risk.

entries.short_title: Orients through authenticity, meaning, and difference

sections.title: The overall pattern
sections.lead: If this candidate fits, attention may repeatedly return to meaning, authenticity, what is missing, and the texture of personal experience.
paragraphs: You may first register whether an experience feels authentic, meaningful, and accurately yours, with particular sensitivity to what is absent or off-key. Emotional richness alone is insufficient; the question is whether difference repeatedly organizes choice.

Wanting accurate understanding is not the same as wanting to be special, and it may arise from a particular relationship or creative task. Stable engagement in ordinary, repetitive life is important counterevidence.
points: Repeatedly noticing meaning, difference, absence, and the texture of experience supports this candidate more than one isolated behavior.
If creative work or a recent experience of loss explains the pattern better, a stable type hypothesis deserves less weight.

sections.title: What draws attention and what you protect
sections.lead: You may notice meaning, authenticity, what is missing, and the texture of personal experience earlier than people around you and allocate effort from there.
paragraphs: You may first sense whether something fits inner experience and contains the meaning that matters before deciding how much to invest. A subtle mismatch can outweigh broad acceptability.
The protected concern may be keeping experience from being flattened. Ease with ordinary, shared work that requires no distinctive expression broadens the account.

sections.title: Outer expression and the need beneath it
sections.lead: The visible move may be to identify feeling and difference before joining a shared rhythm; the less spoken need may be to feel accurately understood while sustaining self-connection in ordinary life.
paragraphs: Under pressure, you may focus more intensely on difference, compare yourself with others, search for a truer expression, or pull away from ordinary tasks. That can protect nuance, but it can also delay action and reality-checking. This is an observable tendency, not a diagnosis.
Nuance or emotional intensity may be heard as dissatisfaction, self-focus, or unwillingness to move on. Treat that as a possible communication gap and check what meaning you wanted to protect.
points: The visible move may be to deepen feeling and seek identity-congruent expression; its purpose still requires contextual and first-person evidence.
Even when the aim is to be accurately understood without losing authenticity, another person’s reported impact remains independent evidence.

sections.lead: A possible habitual sequence is to feel misunderstood, magnify what is absent, compare or imagine, and delay concrete movement.

The pause before you deepen feeling and seek identity-congruent expression is the point where another response may still be available.

sections.lead: A mistyping risk is that creative training, grief, or a period of identity exploration can resemble this search for distinctiveness.
paragraphs: You may treat a strong feeling as proof that a situation has one meaning. Separate the feeling, the facts, and the story you are telling before deciding what action fits.

If Four doesn't emerge as a major clue this time, think of it as a less prominent pattern: Watch to see if you're less proactive in using authenticity, nuance, and unique perspective to calibrate your choices when you need to express differences, identify emotions, or illustrate personal meaning. It is not a judgment that you lack depth or have no self.
points: Attention to meaning, difference, absence, and the texture of experience across work, relationships, and private choices carries more weight than behavior in one role.
Keep creative work or a recent experience of loss as a serious competing explanation.
sections.reflection_question: Around the distinction between a genuine need from intensified attention to what is absent, which evidence repeats across settings, and which similar behavior is better explained by role, culture, temporary strain, or a learned habit?

sections.title: Recurring relationship difficulties
sections.lead: A recurring relationship difficulty may be to move between approach and withdrawal while testing whether understanding is deep enough.
paragraphs: You may want the other person to understand in detail, but in relationships, you can often only understand a part of it first. Start by explaining what you most want to be heard, and give the other person room to ask questions and calibrate.

Emphasis on a detail, difference, or memory may signal what feels meaningful in the relationship, while the current event may also have heightened its importance. Reflect what you heard, then ask what response would be useful now.

Boundaries, power, and communication history may explain the conflict better than attention to meaning, difference, absence, and the texture of experience.

Repair goals, ownership, and communication design before ruling out a coordination role or a situation that truly needs de-escalation.
sections.reflection_question: In a recent collaboration friction involving useful coordination from lowering your own priority, was the missing ingredient information, feedback design, ownership, or psychological safety? What evidence shows that type need not explain it?

sections.title: Leading and being led: authority, boundaries, and interaction
sections.lead: Around authority, you may coordinate inclusively when leading and need gentle but definite priorities and follow-through when led.
paragraphs: When you're in a position of alignment, influence can come from muting the noise, embracing dissent, and allowing the rhythm to be uninterrupted by mood swings. It prompts integrated influence clues, which does not mean that you are naturally suitable for leadership, nor does it mean that team differences can only be resolved through gentleness in the long term.

When someone needs your opinion, giving the question, context, and alternative expressions in advance may make it easier for your true thoughts to emerge. It indicates a low-pressure expression of preference and does not mean that you lack a stance or can only passively cooperate.
points: Clear authority makes it less necessary to stay connected while making personal priority visible through guessing or repeated escalation.
Explicit decision rights and stopping conditions help prevent the pattern from starting to trade personal priority for immediate ease.
sections.reflection_question: In delegating, leading, or being managed when people move at conflicting speeds, friction appears, or your position may disturb the balance, which authority or stopping condition remained unclear? What observable outcome would change if it were explicit?

sections.title: How the habit intensifies or changes under pressure
sections.lead: As pressure rises, you may shift into secondary tasks, slow action, and appear agreeable while resisting internally.
paragraphs: The more an issue requires a position or a difficult choice, the easier it becomes to postpone.
Organizing, scrolling, or low-effort work takes over while the important decision remains untouched.
points: Pressure may amplify the impulse to absorb disagreement, lower tension, and postpone a position until it begins to trade personal priority for immediate ease.
Sleep, workload, and a coordination role or a situation that truly needs de-escalation must be checked alongside a type hypothesis.
sections.reflection_question: As pressure rose when people move at conflicting speeds, friction appears, or your position may disturb the balance, which action intensified first? What did it protect, when did it narrow choice, and could sleep, workload, or real risk explain it better?

sections.title: What becomes possible when safety increases
sections.lead: With more safety, you may recognize preferences sooner, decide proactively, and tolerate short-term disagreement.
paragraphs: You may bring patience and continuity to work that depends on steady maintenance rather than short bursts of novelty.
You may understand competing positions without requiring yourself to surrender your own.
points: When safety increases, the impulse to absorb disagreement, lower tension, and postpone a position is no longer the only familiar response.
Look for flexibility while attending to overall stability, other viewpoints, friction cost, and familiar pace, not evidence that you have become another type.
sections.reflection_question: When you felt safe and unhurried, did a different response appear—for example, the relationship holds after you state a disagreement? How could you tell that safety, rather than a different task, accounted for the change?

sections.title: Growth means adding choice, not becoming another type
sections.lead: Growth can mean learning to occupy space promptly while preserving connection through small, explicit choices.
paragraphs: In one small decision this week, state your preference, your reason, and what remains negotiable. If you need time, say exactly when you will return to the discussion.
Start with a low-stakes choice and practice making your position visible.
points: Growth adds an optional step before you absorb disagreement, lower tension, and postpone a position; it does not require erasing the original tendency.
Use seven days of evidence to test whether the new choice can stay connected while making personal priority visible without the familiar cost.
sections.reflection_question: The next time when people move at conflicting speeds, friction appears, or your position may disturb the balance, what small choice could you add without discarding your existing strength? What behavioral evidence after seven days would count as useful?

sections.title: The nine theoretical levels of development
sections.lead: The nine levels are a theoretical reading framework. For Type 9, The Peacemaker, they can organize observations about how overall stability, shared pace, friction, and every party’s place changes with resources and pressure, but this score cannot locate you at a level.
paragraphs: Level language describes a range of expression; it is not a health grade, diagnosis, or ranking of personal worth.
Use concrete behavior, duration, contextual resources, and counterexamples, and seek appropriate professional support when needed.
points: Theory observation axis: overall stability, shared pace, friction, and every party’s place
Automatic assignment to any level is prohibited
Scores do not establish health, maturity, or clinical status

sections.title: Early signals and routes back to choice
sections.lead: Early signals may include saying “anything is fine,” choosing low-priority tasks, or repeatedly delaying a decision.
paragraphs: Start with one low-conflict statement: name your current preference or minimum position without trying to resolve the whole disagreement.
Begin with ‘I currently prefer…’ without requiring yourself to make a final decision.
points: When you first begin to trade personal priority for immediate ease, bodily, behavioral, and relational signals often arrive before the later explanation.
Recovery restores choice while checking whether a coordination role or a situation that truly needs de-escalation still requires practical or professional support.
sections.reflection_question: For moments when people move at conflicting speeds, friction appears, or your position may disturb the balance, name one bodily, one behavioral, and one relational early signal. Which low-cost recovery step comes first, and when would another form of support be appropriate?

growth_actions.title: State your preference first in one small decision
growth_actions.instruction: Each day, state your preference first in one small decision, including the option and timing, before hearing others. Do not withdraw it with “anything is fine.”
growth_actions.observable_outcome: Record response time, the other person’s actual reaction, and the final choice. Test whether difference truly damaged connection.

growth_actions.title: Put the most important task in the first work block
growth_actions.instruction: Place the most important task in the first available block and close one habitual activity before starting. Require only a minimum advance rather than the right overall mood.
growth_actions.observable_outcome: Compare progress, reduction in routine activity, and energy. Identify the trigger that most often removes the priority from view.

growth_actions.title: Set a firm deadline for one delayed decision
growth_actions.instruction: For one delayed decision, set a date, required information, and a default option at expiry. Once information is sufficient, do not use further coordination to postpone choice.
growth_actions.observable_outcome: Record whether the deadline held, the cost of delay, and unresolved disagreement. Allow only one replacement date with a written reason.

growth_actions.title: Restate what you genuinely agree to before saying yes
growth_actions.instruction: Before agreeing, repeat what you will own, what you will not own, and what the other person must carry. Wait for confirmation before beginning.
growth_actions.observable_outcome: Check whether the commitment stayed clear, whether resentment or forgetting decreased, and whether you expanded scope merely to restore harmony.

growth_actions.title: Record one disagreement that the relationship survived
growth_actions.instruction: Track the twenty-four hours after voicing one disagreement: the response, relationship change, and issue progress. Do not use immediate tension to predict permanent rupture.
growth_actions.observable_outcome: Compare expected and actual consequences, keeping evidence of continued stability alongside facts that require repair or a renewed boundary.
